newsitem.title: USA: Dow ends volatile week up as bonds rise before FOMC meeting.
newsitem.headline: Dow ends volatile week up as bonds rise before FOMC meeting.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks surged more than 100 points before ending with modest gains on Friday, snapping a two-session losing streak at the close of a week of volatile trading on Wall Street.

A firm bond market, investor conviction that the Federal Reserve will not raise interest rates at a policy meeting next week and buying by portfolio managers at the end of the quarter supported stocks, traders said.
The Dow Jones industrial average finished up 33.47 points, or 0.44 percent, at 7,687.72. The index had been as many as 116 points higher before late-session profit-taking shaved the gains.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines by a margin of 1,799 to 938 on the New York Stock Exchange on active volume of 469.7 million shares.

For the week the Dow finished with a loss of 108.79 points, or 1.5 percent. This came after a near 200-point drop Monday triggered by remarks from Japan's prime minister on possible Japanese selling of U.S. Treasury bonds and a rebound of more than 150 points on Tuesday.
"Nothing much has happened, but you've travelled a lot of miles in between," said Alfred Kugel, senior investment strategist at Stein Roe & Farnham.
The Dow ended last week at a record high of 7,796.51, a 22 percent rise from its 1997 closing low at 6,391.69 on April 11.
Market analysts attributed this week's sharp swings to a general nervousness among investors holding big gains after the 10-week rise of over 1,400 points.
"That's what the volatility shows," said James Melcher, president of Balestra Capital. The stock market "is edgy all right, and it ought to be."
On Friday stocks got support from bonds, which broke out of a week-long slide, lifted by the Fed's unexpected purchase in the market of U.S. Treasuries with longer maturities.
The 30-year Treasury bond rose 14/32, its yield dropping to 6.75 percent from Thursday's close at 6.78 percent.
Wall Street's next hurdle will come Tuesday and Wednesday when the Fed's Federal Open Market Committee will meet on interest-rate policy.
The consensus on Wall Street is that the central bank will leave rates unchanged.
"If the Fed does anything, it will be a big surprise to the Street," said Brian Finnerty, senior vice president at Unterberg Harris.
Among individual issues, NationsBank Corp. fell 1-3/8 to 65-1/4 amid reports it would soon announce it will buy closely held investment bank Montgomery Securities.
Another investment bank, Hambrecht & Quist Inc., fell 1-7/8 to 32-1/4 after a Smith Barney analyst downgraded his rating on the stock, saying recent takeover speculation had bloated its share price.

Two initial public stock offerings attracted buyers. JLK Direct Distribution Inc., distributors of metal cutting tools, rose 5-1/2 to 25-1/2. Heating and air conditioning company Comfort Systems USA Inc. rose three to 16.

PacifiCare Health Systems Inc. fell sharply for the second time this week, warning that profits would be sharply below expectations. The health maintenance organisation cited substantially higher health care costs in a number of markets.
Its Class A shares sank 6-1/2 to 59-3/8. On Tuesday they dropped 17-1/4 points after an initial profit warning.
The Nasdaq composite index ended 1.77 points higher at 1,438.15, but fell 8.95 from last Friday.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks edged up 3.62 to 887.30, down 11.41 on the week. The American Stock Exchange index rose 3.97 points to 620.07, down 3.2 from last Friday.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 2.37 to 463.30. For the week it dropped 4.54. The average price per share rose 22 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was at 8,399.764, up 35.395 or 0.42 percent. The index was down 84.746 on the week.
